title: REDUCE – Reduced radiological and biopsy diagnostics in the primary diagnosis of prostate cancer: A prospective randomized non-inferiority intervention study comparing target plus systematic biopsy versus target plus peri-sensional biopsy
summary:
For the early detection of prostate cancer, men first undergo a blood test. This test measures a specific value that can indicate a disease of the prostate. If this value is repeatedly elevated, an examination using magnetic resonance imaging is usually performed. This imaging method produces detailed pictures of the prostate and helps identify suspicious areas. In addition, a physical examination of the prostate through the rectum and an ultrasound examination may be carried out.

If the imaging shows a suspicious area, a tissue sample from the prostate is recommended. During this procedure, several small tissue samples are taken using a thin needle inserted through the skin between the scrotum and the anus. The sampling is guided by imaging to ensure that suspicious areas are specifically targeted.

Currently, there are two commonly used approaches for taking these tissue samples.
In the first approach, in addition to the targeted samples from the suspicious area, further samples are taken from several predefined regions of the prostate.
In the second approach, in addition to the targeted samples, only extra samples from the immediate surrounding area of the suspicious region are taken.

Both approaches are recommended in Germany and other European countries and are used in routine medical practice. However, for the second method, there is no standardized rule defining exactly how many additional samples should be taken and from which precise locations. This decision is currently left to the treating physician.

Previous studies have shown that most clinically relevant prostate cancers are located within about one centimeter of the suspicious area seen on imaging. By taking additional samples within this radius, it may be possible to reduce the total number of samples needed without missing important cancers. At the same time, this approach may reduce the detection of very small tumors that may not require treatment.

After the procedure, the tissue samples are examined under a microscope by specialists in pathology. The examination determines whether cancer cells are present and how aggressive the tumor appears to be. It also assesses how much of each sample is affected and whether the tumor may have spread beyond the prostate.

Purpose of the Study

The aim of this study is to compare the two recommended biopsy approaches. The study will evaluate:

how often clinically relevant prostate cancer is detected,

how often tumors are found that may not require treatment,

patient satisfaction during the procedure,

the level of pain experienced during the procedure,

and any side effects occurring after the procedure.

All examinations and treatments are part of routine medical care. Before the biopsy, participants will be randomly assigned to one of the two approaches. The results will then be observed and analyzed over a defined period of time. Care will be taken to ensure that both groups are comparable in terms of age, blood test results, and imaging findings.

The study aims to determine whether the approach with fewer additional tissue samples is as reliable as the method currently widely used in Germany, which involves taking a larger number of samples. The overall goal is to make prostate cancer diagnosis as safe, accurate, and gentle as possible for patients.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Biparametric magnetic resonance imaging performed at the University Hospital Bonn to ensure uniform quality standards.

Adequate image quality with imaging performed in accordance with version 2.1 of the Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System and a Prostate Imaging Quality score of at least 2 out of 3.

The patient provides written informed consent to participate in the study.

Patients who are able to follow study instructions and are likely to attend all required study visits (compliance).
Exclusion criteria:
The patient has a prostate-specific antigen level greater than 25 ng/ml with suspicion of primarily metastatic prostate cancer.
